title: BETHANECOL Direct Acting Muscarinic Agonist
action:
Direct-acting muscarinic agonist that selectively binds to and activates muscarinic
acetylcholine receptors, stimulating the parasympathetic nervous system. It increases tone in the bladder
detrusor muscle to prompt urination and enhances gastrointestinal smooth muscle tone and peristalsis.
forms:
Oral tablets:
5 mg, 10 mg, 25 mg,
50 mg.
Subcutaneous injection:
5 mg/mL.
indication:
Treatment of acute
postoperative and
postpartum
nonobstructive
(functional) urinary
retention, and
neurogenic atony of
the urinary bladder
with retention.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity, mechanical
gastrointestinal or urinary
obstruction,
hyperthyroidism, peptic
ulcer disease, active or
latent bronchial asthma,
pronounced bradycardia,
hypotension, and coronary
artery disease.
adverse:
Severe drop in blood
pressure with reflex
tachycardia, syncope,
bronchospasm, heart
block, and cardiac
arrest.
effects:
Abdominal discomfort,
cramps, excessive
salivation, diarrhea,
nausea, vomiting,
sweating, flushing,
headache, and urinary
urgency.
notes:
Should be taken on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after meals) to minimize nausea and vomiting. Atropine
sulfate is the specific antidote for overdosage.

title: PILOCARPINE Direct Acting Muscarinic Agonist
action:
Direct-acting cholinergic parasympathomimetic agent that stimulates muscarinic
receptors, causing contraction of the iris sphincter (miosis) and ciliary muscle, and stimulation of
exocrine (salivary) glands.
forms:
Ophthalmic solution:
0.5%, 1%, 2%, 3%,
4%, 6%.
Ophthalmic gel: 4%.
Oral tablets (saligen):
5 mg.
indication:
Management of chronic
open-angle glaucoma,
acute angle-closure
glaucoma, and
treatment of symptoms
of xerostomia (dry
mouth) caused by
salivary gland
hypofunction or
Sjögren’s syndrome.
contraindication:
Acute inflammation of
the anterior chamber,
hypersensitivity,
secondary glaucoma
where constriction is
undesirable, and
uncontrolled asthma
or severe acute
cardiac disease.
adverse:
Retinal detachment,
paradoxical increase in
intraocular pressure, and
systemic cholinergic
toxicity (hypotension,
bronchospasm).
effects:
Blurred vision, decreased
night vision, brow ache,
eye irritation, lacrimation,
increased sweating,
flushing, and rhinitis.
notes:
Caution patients about driving or performing hazardous
tasks at night due to impaired vision from miosis.

title: MUSCARINE Direct Acting Muscarinic Agonist
action:
A natural, potent direct-acting muscarinic receptor agonist that mimics
acetylcholine at parasympathetic neuroeffector junctions, leading to excessive
parasympathetic overstimulation.
forms:
Not an FDA-approved
pharmaceutical drug;
available strictly as a research
toxin or standard reference
compound (isolated naturally
from Amanita muscaria and
other mushrooms)
indication:
None clinically
approved (used
primarily in
pharmacological
research to study
muscarinic
pathways).
contraindication:
N/A (Toxin; not
used
therapeutically).
adverse:
Severe cholinergic poisoning
profile (SLUDGE:
Salivation, Lacrimation,
Urination, Defecation,
Gastrointestinal distress,
Emesis), severe miosis,
extreme bradycardia,
hypotension, and fatal
bronchoconstriction.
effects:
Profuse sweating,
excessive salivation,
blurred vision,
abdominal cramping,
and severe vomiting.
notes:
Muscarine is not broken down by acetylcholinesterase,
contributing to its high toxicity proﬁle. Treated medically with
atropine as an antidote.

title: NICOTINE
action:
Binds to and stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the central nervous system,
adrenal medulla, autonomic ganglia, and neuromuscular junctions, prompting the release of dopamine and
other neurotransmitters
forms:
Transdermal patches: 7 mg/24hr, 14
mg/24hr, 21 mg/24hr.
Chewing gum/lozenges: 2 mg, 4 mg.
Inhaler: 10 mg cartridge.
Nasal spray: 10 mg/mL.
indication:
Nicotine replacement
therapy (NRT) for
smoking cessation
and relief of nicotine
withdrawal
symptoms.
contraindication:
Immediate post-myocardial
infarction period, severe or
worsening angina pectoris,
severe cardiac arrhythmias,
and active temporal/jaw
TMJ disorders (for gum)
adverse:
Tachycardia, hypertension,
cardiac arrhythmias, and
acute nicotine toxicity
(seizures, respiratory
failure).
effects:
Local skin irritation (patch),
mouth irritation or hiccups
(gum/lozenge), insomnia,
headache, dizziness, nausea,
and vivid dreams.
notes:
Advise patients to completely stop smoking while using any
nicotine replacement product to avoid dangerous cardiovascular
spikes

title: VARENICLINE
action:
Partial agonist-antagonist that binds selectively to alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic
acetylcholine receptors, reducing feelings of pleasure derived from nicotine while alleviating
withdrawal symptoms.
forms:
Oral tablets: 0.5 mg and 1 mg
(often sold in continuation or
starting starter packs).
indication:
Adjunctive aid
for smoking
cessation
treatment in
adults.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivit
y to varenicline
or its
excipients.
adverse:
Serious neuropsychiatric events
(changes in behavior,
depression, suicidal ideation),
severe skin reactions (Stevens-
Johnson syndrome), and
cardiovascular events in high-
risk patients.
effects:
Nausea (most common),
insomnia, abnormal/vivid
dreams, constipation,
flatulence, and dry mouth.
notes:
Should be taken with food and a full glass of water to help
minimize treatment-related nausea.

title: SUCCINYLCHOLINE
action:
A depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant. It mimics acetylcholine, binding to nicotinic
receptors at the neuromuscular junction to cause prolonged depolarization, rendering the motor end-plate
resistant to further activation by ACh.
forms:
Solution for injection /
IV infusion:
20 mg/mL, 50 mg/mL,
100 mg/mL.
indication:
Adjunct to general
anesthesia to facilitate
endotracheal intubation
and to relax skeletal
muscles during surgery
or mechanical
ventilation.
contraindication:
Personal or family history
of malignant
hyperthermia, major
burns, massive skeletal
muscle trauma, extensive
denervation of skeletal
muscle, and pre-existing
hyperkalemia.
adverse:
Malignant hyperthermia,
severe hyperkalemia (which
can cause cardiac arrest),
cardiac arrhythmias, and
prolonged apnea.
effects:
Postoperative muscle
fasciculations and
transient muscle pain
(myalgia).
notes:
Has a rapid onset (under 1 minute) and very short duration
of action (5 to 10 minutes). Must be administered only by
personnel skilled in airway management.

title: ENDROPHONIUM
action:
A short-acting reversible indirect-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It reversibly binds to the active
center of acetylcholinesterase, temporarily preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine and amplifying cholinergic
effects at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptor sites.
forms:
Intravenous/
Intramuscula
r injection:
10 mg/mL.
indication:
Differential diagnosis of
myasthenia gravis (Tensilon
test) and evaluation of acute
myasthenic crises vs.
cholinergic crises; also used as
a temporary reversal agent for
non-depolarizing
neuromuscular blocking
drugs.
contraindication:
Known
hypersensitivity,
mechanical
intestinal or urinary
obstruction.
adverse:
Severe bradycardia,
laryngospasm,
bronchoconstriction, and
cardiac arrhythmias or
arrest
effects:
Increased salivation,
lacrimation,
diaphoresis, nausea,
vomiting, abdominal
cramps, and miosis.
notes:
Due to its ultra-short duration of action (about 5–10 minutes) and the risk of profound
bradycardia, an antagonist like atropine sulfate must always be immediately
available during administration.

title: NEOSTIGMINE
action:
Reversible indirect-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that forms a covalent carbamyl-enzyme
complex, inhibiting the breakdown of acetylcholine and increasing its availability at neuromuscular junctions and
autonomic synapses.
forms:
Solution for injection:
0.5 mg/mL, 1 mg/mL.
Oral tablets: 15 mg.
indication:
Reversal of effects of non-
depolarizing
neuromuscular blocking
agents after surgery;
symptomatic
management of
myasthenia gravis.
contraindication:
Peritonitis,
mechanical
obstruction of the
intestinal or
urinary tract, and
known
hypersensitivity.
adverse:
Severe bronchospasm,
cardiovascular depression,
bradycardia, and
cholinergic crisis.
effects:
Muscle twitching, excessive
salivation, nausea, vomiting,
diarrhea, abdominal cramps,
and urinary frequency.
notes:
Often administered alongside an anticholinergic agent (such as
atropine or glycopyrrolate) to block unwanted muscarinic side
eﬀects like severe bradycardia.

title: PYRIDOSTIGMINE
action:
Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that prolongs the action of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular
junction. It has a longer duration of action compared to neostigmine.
forms:
Oral tablets: 60 mg.
Extended-release tablets: 180
mg. Syrup: 60 mg/5 mL.
Injection: 5 mg/mL.
indication:
Long-term treatment
of myasthenia gravis
and prophylaxis
against nerve agents
(such as Soman) in
military settings.
contraindication:
Mechanical obstruction
of the gastrointestinal
or urinary tract, and
hypersensitivity to
anticholinesterase
agents.
adverse:
Syncope, seizures,
severe bradycardia,
bronchospasm, and
dysrhythmias.
effects:
Muscle cramps, increased
bronchial secretions,
excessive sweating,
diarrhea, nausea, and
abdominal discomfort
notes:
Dosage must be carefully titrated to the individual patient to
balance therapeutic weakness relief against the onset of a
cholinergic crisis.

title: PHYSOSTIGMINE
action:
Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Unlike other carbamates, it contains a tertiary amine structure,
allowing it to readily cross the blood-brain barrier and treat central nervous system effects.
forms:
Solution for injection:
1 mg/mL.
indication:
Treatment of severe
anticholinergic toxicity
(e.g., overdose from
atropine, scopolamine, or
tricyclic antidepressants).
contraindication:
Asthma, gangrene, diabetes,
cardiovascular disease,
mechanical obstruction of
the intestinal or urinary
tract, and poisoning by
depolarizing
neuromuscular blockers.
adverse:
Seizures, hypersalivation
leading to respiratory
compromise,
bradycardia, asystole,
and bronchospasm.
effects:
Nausea, vomiting,
sweating, dizziness,
and restlessness.
notes:
Administer via slow IV injection to prevent cardiac arrhythmias and
seizures. Atropine should be on hand as a reversing agent if severe
cholinergic side eﬀects emerge.

title: PARATHION
action:
Irreversible organophosphate acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It phosphorylates the active site of the enzyme,
permanently deactivating it and causing a massive accumulation of acetylcholine across all cholinergic synapses.
forms:
Agricultural/industrial
formulations (restricted-use
pesticide; not an approved
clinical pharmaceutical
drug).
indication:
None clinically
(historically used
exclusively as an
agricultural
insecticide/pesticide).
contraindication:
N/A (Highly toxic chemical
agent; contraindicated for
any medical or household
use due to extreme
mammalian toxicity).
adverse:
Fatal respiratory failure,
severe pulmonary edema,
uncontrollable convulsions,
profound bradycardia,
complete neuromuscular
paralysis, and death.
effects:
Profuse sweating, excessive
lacrimation, uncontrollable
diarrhea, vomiting, muscle
fasciculations, miosis, and
confusion.
notes:
Highly absorbed through skin, lungs, and the GI tract. Treated aggressively with
decontamination, high-dose atropine (to block muscarinic signs), and
pralidoxime (2-PAM) to regenerate acetylcholinesterase if administered early.

title: MALATHION
action:
Organophosphate acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. In mammals, it is biotransformed to malaoxon, inhibiting
acetylcholinesterase, though it has a lower systemic mammalian toxicity than parathion.
forms:
Topical lotion/shampoo:
0.5% (Ovide).
Agricultural formulations
vary.
indication:
Treatment of head
lice and their ova
(eggs) via topical
application.
contraindication:
Neonates and infants
(due to potential for
increased skin
absorption and
neurotoxicity), and
known
hypersensitivity.
adverse:
Local chemical burns, skin
irritation, stinging, and
systemic toxicity if
ingested or excessively
absorbed through broken
skin.
effects:
Scalp irritation, erythema,
and temporary increase
in localized sweating.
notes:
Flammable formulation; patients must keep away from open
ﬂames or hair dryers while the product is wet on the hair.

title: SARIN, TABUN, others
action:
Extremely potent, irreversible organophosphate nerve agents. They covalently bind to the active serine
site of acetylcholinesterase, leading to permanent enzyme inactivation and a toxic, lethal flood of acetylcholine throughout the
central and peripheral nervous systems.
forms:
Not a pharmaceutical
drug; chemical
warfare agents.
indication:
None (classified strictly
as weapons of mass
destruction / chemical
warfare agents).
contraindication: N/A.
adverse:
Rapid loss of consciousness,
violent convulsions, copious
airway secretions, immediate
respiratory muscle paralysis,
asphyxiation, and death.
effects:
Sudden pin-point pupils
(miosis), extreme
rhinorrhea, intense
dyspnea, and uncontrolled
body secretions.
notes:
Extremely lethal via inhalation or minimal skin contact. Immediate emergency response
requires removal from exposure, decontamination, and prompt administration of
atropine and pralidoxime alongside an anticonvulsant like diazepam.

title: RIVERSTIGMINE
action:
Dual inhibitor of both acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase
(pseudocholinesterase) in the brain, helping to increase cortical levels of acetylcholine.
forms:
Oral capsules:
1.5 mg, 3 mg, 4.5 mg, 6 mg.
Oral solution: 2 mg/mL.
Transdermal patches: 4.6 mg/24hr,
9.5 mg/24hr, 13.3 mg/24hr.
indication:
Treatment of mild to
moderate dementia of
the Alzheimer's type
and mild to moderate
dementia associated
with Parkinson's
disease.
contraindication:
Known hypersensitivity
to rivastigmine, other
carbamate derivatives,
or previous history of
application-site
contact dermatitis
with the rivastigmine
patch.
adverse:
Severe bradycardia, syncopal
episodes, gastrointestinal
hemorrhage, and worsening
of extrapyramidal
symptoms.
effects:
Nausea, vomiting,
anorexia, weight loss,
abdominal pain,
dizziness, asthenia, and
insomnia.
notes:
Oral forms should be taken with food (breakfast and dinner) to
reduce gastrointestinal side eﬀects. Patches should be applied daily
to clean, dry, hairless skin and rotated to avoid skin irritation.

title: GALANTAMINE
action:
A reversible, competitive acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that also acts as an
allosteric modulator at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, enhancing the action of acetylcholine at
nicotinic sites.
forms:
Oral tablets: 4 mg, 8 mg, 12 mg.
Extended-release capsules: 8 mg,
16 mg, 24 mg.
Oral solution: 4 mg/mL.
indication:
Treatment of mild to
moderate dementia
of the Alzheimer's
type.
contraindication:
Severe renal impairment
(creatinine clearance
less than 9 mL/min) and
severe hepatic
impairment.
adverse:
Slowed heart rate
(bradycardia), heart block,
syncope, gastrointestinal
bleeding, and increased
risk of seizures.
effects:
Nausea, vomiting,
diarrhea, weight loss,
decreased appetite,
dizziness, headache, and
fatigue.
notes:
Take with food and ensure adequate ﬂuid intake during
treatment to minimize GI side eﬀects. Titrate dosage slowly over
intervals of at least 4 weeks.

title: DONEPAZIL
action:
Highly selective, reversible inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase, increasing the concentration of acetylcholine
available in synaptic clefts within the central nervous system.
forms:
Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg, 23 mg.
Orally disintegrating tablets (ODT):
5 mg, 10 mg.
indication:
Treatment of mild,
moderate, to severe
dementia of the
Alzheimer's type.
contraindication:
Known hypersensitivity to
donepezil or piperidine
derivatives
adverse:
Syncope, severe bradycardia,
QT prolongation,
gastrointestinal ulceration,
and upper GI bleeding.
effects:
Vivid dreams, insomnia,
diarrhea, muscle cramps,
fatigue, nausea, and
vomiting.
notes:
Usually taken once daily at bedtime, with or without food. It has a
long half-life (about 70 hours), making once-daily dosing
convenient for chronic compliance.

title: ATROPINE
action:
Competitive, non-selective muscarinic receptor antagonist that blocks the effects
of acetylcholine at parasympathetic neuroeffector sites on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and
secretory glands.
forms:
Injection: 0.1 mg/mL, 0.4 mg/
mL, 0.5 mg/mL, 1 mg/mL.
Ophthalmic solution: 1%.
Eye ointment: 1%
indication:
Preoperative medication to reduce
salivary and bronchial
secretions, treatment of
symptomatic bradycardia,
resuscitation during asystole,
and as an antidote for
organophosphate or nerve
agent poisoning.
contraindication:
Glaucoma (narrow-angle),
obstructive gastrointestinal
disease, obstructive uropathy,
paralytic ileus, toxic
megacolon, and tachycardia
secondary to cardiac
insufficiency or thyrotoxicosis.
adverse:
Ventricular fibrillation, acute
psychosis, severe
paradoxical bradycardia
(with low doses), and
anaphylaxis.
effects:
Xerostomia (dry mouth),
blurred vision, photophobia,
tachycardia, constipation,
urinary retention, and
flushing.
notes:
Frequently used as the primary antidote for acute cholinergic
toxicity (antidote for organophosphates, carbamates, and
muscarinic mushroom poisoning)

title:
DOREFENACIN, FESOTERODIN, SOLIFENACIN,
TLTERODINE
action:
Competitive muscarinic receptor antagonists that display relative selectivity for the urinary bladder over
salivary glands, reducing bladder smooth muscle contractions and detrusor pressure.
forms:
• Darifenacin (ER): 7.5 mg, 15 mg tablets.
• Fesoterodine (ER): 4 mg, 8 mg tablets.
• Solifenacin: 5 mg, 10 mg tablets.
• Tolterodine: 1 mg, 2 mg tablets;
ER capsules: 2 mg, 4 mg.
indication:
Overactive bladder
(OAB) associated with
symptoms of urge
urinary incontinence,
urgency, and urinary
frequency
contraindication:
Urinary retention, gastric
retention, uncontrolled
narrow-angle glaucoma,
and severe hepatic
impairment (for certain
agents).
adverse:
Severe urinary retention,
QT prolongation
(especially tolterodine
and fesoterodine), and
angioedema.
effects:
Dry mouth, constipation,
dyspepsia, blurred
vision, dry eyes, and
headache.
notes:
Extended-release formulations help reduce peak-to-trough
ﬂuctuations and lower the incidence of dry mouth compared to
immediate-release formulations.

title: PIRENZEPINE, TELENZEPINE
action:
Selective antagonists of M_1 muscarinic receptors located in gastric parietal cells and
enteric ganglia, which significantly reduces gastric acid secretion and pepsin output without heavily affecting
general smooth muscle or cardiac functions.
forms:
Oral tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg
(Pirenzepine; availability
varies by country/region).
indication:
Adjunctive treatment for
peptic ulcer disease and
gastric hyperacidity
disorders.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
antimuscarinics,
mechanical intestinal
obstruction, pyloric
stenosis, and active
gastrointestinal
hemorrhage.
adverse:
Marked visual
disturbances,
precipitation of
glaucoma, and
severe allergic
reactions.
effects:
Mild dry mouth,
transient blurred
vision, constipation,
and mild drowsiness.
notes:
These are considered older or regional agents designed to target
gastric acid secretion while minimizing typical systemic side eﬀects
(like severe tachycardia) seen with nonselective agents.

title: ACLIDINIUM
action:
Long-acting, competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
(M_3 receptors in airway smooth muscle), causing bronchodilation.
forms:
Inhalation powder (Genuair/
Pressair inhaler): 400 mcg
per actuation.
indication:
Long-term, maintenance
treatment of bronchospasm
associated with chronic
obstructive pulmonary
disease (COPD), including
chronic bronchitis and
emphysema.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
aclidinium or atropine
derivatives; acute
treatment of acute
bronchospasm episodes
(rescue therapy).
adverse:
Immediate hypersensitivity
reactions (including
angioedema and urticaria),
paradoxical
bronchospasm.
effects:
Nasopharyngitis,
headache, cough,
sinusitis, and mild
dry mouth.
notes:
Rapidly hydrolyzed in human plasma, which minimizes systemic
side eﬀects. Not a rescue medication.

title: IPRATROPIUM
action:
Short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA) that blocks acetylcholine at M_3
receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, preventing cyclic GMP-mediated bronchoconstriction and
excessive mucus secretion.
forms:
Inhalation aerosol (MDI):
17 mcg/actuation.
Nasal spray: 0.03%, 0.06%.
Solution for nebulization:
0.02%.
indication:
Maintenance treatment of
bronchospasm
associated with COPD
and asthma; acute
exacerbations of asthma
or COPD (often
combined with
albuterol); rhinorrhea.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
ipratropium,
atropine, or its
derivatives.
adverse:
Paradoxical bronchospasm,
acute angle-closure
glaucoma (if sprayed into
the eyes), and severe
urinary retention.
effects:
Dry mouth, throat
irritation, cough, bitter
taste, and mild
headache.
notes:
Does not cross the blood-brain barrier well, avoiding central
nervous system side eﬀects. Care must be taken to prevent the
aerosol from entering the eyes.

title: TIOTROPIUM
action:
Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA), often referred to as an anticholinergic
bronchodilator. It exhibits slow dissociation from M_3 receptors, providing prolonged bronchodilation
lasting 24 hours.
forms:
Inhalation powder
(HandiHaler): 18 mcg/
capsule.
Soft mist inhaler (Respimat):
1.25 mcg or 2.5 mcg per
actuation.
indication:
Long-term, once-daily
maintenance treatment of
bronchospasm associated
with COPD, and
maintenance treatment of
asthma in patients aged 6
years and older.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity
to tiotropium,
atropine, or
ipratropium.
adverse:
Paradoxical bronchospasm,
worsening of narrow-
angle glaucoma, and acute
urinary retention.
effects:
Dry mouth, upper
respiratory tract infections,
sinusitis, pharyngitis, and
constipation.
notes:
Provides a full 24-hour duration of action, making it a
cornerstone maintenance therapy for COPD management.

title: UMECLIDINIUM
action:
Long-acting antimuscarinic agent that blocks the action of acetylcholine on muscarinic
receptors (M_3) in airway smooth muscle, leading to bronchodilation.
forms:
Inhalation powder
(Ellipta inhaler): 62.5
mcg per actuation.
indication:
Long-term, once-
daily maintenance
treatment of
airflow obstruction
in patients with
COPD.
contraindication:
Severe hypersensitivity
to milk proteins
(lactose) or
umeclidinium
components.
adverse:
Paradoxical
bronchospasm, acute
angle-closure glaucoma
flare-ups, and urinary
retention.
effects:
Nasopharyngitis, upper
respiratory tract
infection, cough,
tachycardia, and dry
mouth.
notes:
Often combined with other agents (such as vilanterol) in ﬁxed-dose
combination inhalers for synergistic bronchodilatory beneﬁts.

title: HEXAMETHONIUM
action:
Non-depolarizing ganglionic blocker that competitively blocks nicotinic
acetylcholine receptors located in both sympathetic and parasympathetic autonomic ganglia.
forms:
Historical drug; rarely or no
longer manufactured for
commercial clinical
distribution.
indication:
Historically used as an
antihypertensive agent
(obsolete due to severe
adverse autonomic
blocking effects).
contraindication:
Severe hypotension,
coronary
insufficiency, and
paralytic ileus.
adverse:
Profound orthostatic
hypotension,
cardiovascular collapse,
paralytic ileus, and
severe urinary retention.
effects:
Cycloplegia, dry mouth,
severe constipation,
impotence, and
dizziness.
notes:
It blocks both sympathetic and parasympathetic outﬂows entirely,
resulting in unpredictable and severe side eﬀects. It is primarily of
historical and pharmacological interest today.

title: TRIMETHAPHAN
action:
Short-acting competitive ganglionic blocking agent that blocks transmission
through autonomic ganglia, causing vasodilation and a marked drop in blood pressure.
forms:
Intravenous
infusion solution:
50 mg/mL.
indication:
Production of controlled
hypotension during
specific surgical
procedures (such as
neurosurgery or repair
of coarctation of the
aorta) and management
of hypertensive
emergencies.
contraindication:
Hypovolemia, shock,
severe anemia,
asphyxia, and
respiratory
insufficiency.
adverse:
Severe, unmanageable
hypotension,
respiratory
depression, and
paralytic ileus.
effects:
Mydriasis,
cycloplegia, urinary
retention, dry mouth,
and cessation of
bowel sounds.
notes:
Administered strictly via continuous IV infusion under close blood
pressure monitoring; eﬀects wear oﬀ rapidly upon discontinuation.

title: MECAMYLAMINE
classification:
Antinicotinic Ganglion Blockers
Antinicotinic Neuromuscular Blockers
action:
Non-selective, non-competitive ganglionic blocker that crosses the blood-
brain barrier readily to block nicotinic receptors in autonomic ganglia and the central nervous
system.
forms:
Oral tablets: 2.5 mg
(historically; current
clinical availability is
specialized/limited).
indication:
Historically used for
moderately severe to
severe essential
hypertension;
investigated as an adjunct
for tobacco smoking
cessation and Tourette's
syndrome.
contraindication:
Coronary thrombosis,
recent myocardial
infarction, uremia,
and organic
cerebral damage.
adverse:
Severe orthostatic
hypotension,
neuromuscular weakness,
and toxic psychosis /
convulsions (due to CNS
penetration).
effects:
Constipation (can progress
to paralytic ileus),
blurred vision, dry
mouth, urinary retention,
and sedation.
notes:
Unlike many other ganglion blockers, it is absorbed well orally
due to its secondary amine structure, which also allows it to enter
the central nervous system easily.

title: PRALIDAXIME
action:
Reactivates acetylcholinesterase that has been inactivated by organophosphate pesticides
or nerve agents. It binds to the organophosphate-enzyme complex, releases the phosphorus atom, and
restores normal enzyme activity.
forms:
Injection: 600 mg/mL auto-
injector, or vials
containing 1 gram of
powder for reconstitution.
indication:
Antidote for poisoning
by organophosphate
pesticides and nerve
agents (used alongside
atropine).
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
pralidoxime; poisoning
by carbaryl or non-
organophosphate
substances (ineffective or
can worsen toxicity).
adverse:
Rapid intravenous
administration can cause
laryngospasm, muscle
rigidity, tachycardia, and
transient neuromuscular
blockade.
effects:
Blurred vision,
dizziness, headache,
nausea, and mild local
pain at the injection
site.
notes:
Must be administered as early as possible after exposure, because
"aging" of the phosphorylated enzyme makes it resistant to
regeneration over time.

title: RUCORONIUM
action:
Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that competitively binds to nicotinic
acetylcholine receptors at the motor end-plate, preventing acetylcholine from binding and causing
skeletal muscle relaxation.
forms:
Intravenous solution:
10 mg/mL.
indication:
Adjunct to general
anesthesia to facilitate
rapid sequence intubation
(RSI) and routine
endotracheal intubation,
and to provide skeletal
muscle relaxation during
surgery.
contraindication:
Known
hypersensitivity to
rocuronium or
bromide-containing
compounds.
adverse:
Anaphylactic/
anaphylactoid
reactions, prolonged
apnea, and severe
bronchospasm.
effects:
Transient injection-site pain
and mild, temporary
changes in heart rate or
blood pressure.
notes:
Features a relatively rapid onset of action compared to other non-depolarizing agents, making it
an alternative to succinylcholine for rapid sequence intubation when depolarizing blockers are
contraindicated. Its effects can be rapidly reversed using sugammadex.

title: ATRACURIUM
action:
Non-depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant that competes with acetylcholine for
nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
forms:
Intravenous solution:
10 mg/mL.
indication:
Adjunct to general
anesthesia to relax
skeletal muscles and
facilitate endotracheal
intubation and
mechanical ventilation
during surgical
procedures.
contraindication:
Known
hypersensitivity to
atracurium or
besylate
components.
adverse:
Histamine release leading
to severe hypotension,
flushing, bronchospasm,
and cardiovascular
collapse.
effects:
Skin flushing, erythema,
transient hypotension,
and mild wheezing.
notes:
Undergoes unique spontaneous degradation in plasma via
Hofmann elimination (independent of liver or kidney function),
making it useful in patients with hepatic or renal failure.

title: MIVACURIUM
action:
Short-acting, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that competitively
blocks nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
forms:
Intravenous solution:
2 mg/mL.
indication:
Adjunct to general
anesthesia for short
surgical procedures
to relax skeletal
muscles and facilitate
tracheal intubation.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
mivacurium and
patients with
homozygous
atypical plasma
cholinesterase
activity.
adverse:
Profound histamine
release causing profound
transient hypotension,
flushing, and
bronchospasm.
effects:
Cutaneous flushing,
transient decrease in
blood pressure, and
mild tachycardia.
notes:
Metabolized primarily by plasma cholinesterase
(pseudocholinesterase); patients with genetic deﬁciencies in this
enzyme experience signiﬁcantly prolonged paralysis.

title: PANCURONIUM BROMIDE
action:
Long-acting, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that competitively
competes with acetylcholine at the motor end-plate.
forms:
Intravenous injection:
1 mg/mL, 2 mg/mL.
indication:
Facilitation of
endotracheal intubation
and provision of skeletal
muscle relaxation during
long surgical procedures
or mechanical
ventilation.
contraindication:
Known hypersensitivity
to pancuronium or
bromides; situations
where tachycardia is
hazardous.
adverse:
Prolonged neuromuscular
blockade, residual
paralysis, and
hypersensitivity reactions.
effects:
Tachycardia (due to vagolytic
action and blockade of cardiac
muscarinic receptors),
hypertension, and increased
salivation.
notes:
Unlike many other muscle relaxants, it typically increases heart
rate and blood pressure instead of dropping it, due to its mild
blocking action on cardiac vagal receptors.

title: TUBOCURARINE
action:
Prototype non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that competitively inhibits
acetylcholine at the skeletal muscle nicotinic receptors.
forms:
Intravenous injection: 3 mg/
mL (Historical/classic
pharmacological agent).
indication:
Historical agent used
as an adjunct to
general anesthesia
for muscle relaxation
and intubation.
contraindication:
Myasthenia gravis,
severe electrolyte
disturbances, and
hypersensitivity.
adverse:
Significant histamine
release causing marked
hypotension, shock-like
symptoms, and
bronchospasm.
effects:
Hypotension,
cutaneous flushing,
respiratory
depression, and
reflex tachycardia.
notes:
Rarely used in modern clinical practice due to its high propensity
for causing histamine-induced hypotension; largely superseded by
safer non-depolarizing agents like rocuronium or atracurium.

title: DEXTROMETORPHAN
action:
Acts centrally on the cough center in the medulla to elevate the threshold for coughing.
(Note: Structurally related to opioids, it acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist and serotonin reuptake
inhibitor at high doses, sitting outside traditional cholinergic pathways).
forms:
Oral syrup: 5 mg/5 mL, 10 mg/5 mL,
15 mg/5 mL.
Lozenges/tablets: 10 mg, 15 mg, 30 mg.
Extended-release suspension:
30 mg/5 mL.
indication:
Temporary relief of
coughs caused by minor
throat and bronchial
irritation (such as that
accompanying a
common cold).
contraindication:
Concurrent use with
monoamine oxidase
inhibitors (MAOIs)
or within 14 days of
stopping them (risk
of severe serotonin
syndrome).
adverse:
Serotonin syndrome (when
combined with
serotonergic drugs), acute
psychosis, and
respiratory depression at
massive toxic/
recreational doses.
effects:
Drowsiness, dizziness,
mild gastrointestinal
upset, and nervousness.
notes:
Widely used over-the-counter antitussive, but listed here as part of
your source sheet context; abuse potential exists at very high supra-
therapeutic doses due to its NMDA antagonist properties.

title: VECURONIUM
action:
Intermediate-acting, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that competitively binds to
nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, blocking the actions of acetylcholine.
forms:
Powder for intravenous
injection: 10 mg/vial,
20 mg/vial.
indication:
Adjunct to general
anesthesia to facilitate
endotracheal intubation
and provide skeletal
muscle relaxation during
surgery or mechanical
ventilation.
contraindication:
Known hypersensitivity
to vecuronium or
bromide-containing
compounds.
adverse:
Prolonged paralysis,
anaphylaxis, and acute
myopathy with
prolonged use in
intensive care settings.
effects:
Minimal hemodynamic
changes, slight
transient changes in
heart rate.
notes:
Lacks signiﬁcant cardiovascular side eﬀects (does not cause
notable histamine release or tachycardia), making it versatile for
patients with cardiac disease. Can be reversed rapidly with
sugammadex.

title: EPINEPHRINE
action:
Non-selective alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist.
It stimulates the heart, relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, and causes systemic vasoconstriction.
forms:
Injection: 1 mg/mL (1:1000)
and 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000).
Auto-injector (EpiPen): 0.3 mg,
0.15 mg.
Inhalation solution: 1%.
indication:
Emergency treatment of
severe allergic
reactions (anaphylaxis),
cardiac arrest, acute
asthma attacks, and
induction of local
anesthesia
prolongation.
contraindication:
Close-angle glaucoma,
shock other than
anaphylactic shock,
known
hypersensitivity, and
during labor (when
vasopressor effects
may delay delivery).
adverse:
Hypertensive crisis,
ventricular arrhythmias,
cerebral hemorrhage,
and pulmonary edema.
effects:
Tachycardia, palpitations,
anxiety, tremor,
headache, and pale
appearance.
notes:
It is the primary drug of choice for acute anaphylaxis; sensitive
to light and air, meaning discolored solutions should be
discarded.

title: NOREPINEPHRINE
action:
Potent alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist, with lesser beta-1 agonist
activity. It causes intense peripheral vasoconstriction and moderate inotropic stimulation of the
heart.
forms:
Intravenous infusion
concentrate: 1 mg/
mL (as base).
indication:
Treatment of severe acute
hypotension and shock
states (e.g., septic
shock, cardiogenic
shock) after fluid
resuscitation.
contraindication:
Mesenteric or peripheral
vascular thrombosis
(unless absolutely
necessary), profound
hypovolemia, and known
hypersensitivity.
adverse:
Severe tissue necrosis upon
extravasation, reflex
bradycardia, severe
hypertension, and decreased
organ perfusion.
effects:
Anxiety, transient headache,
respiratory difficulty, and
bradycardia.
notes:
Must be administered via a central venous catheter when possible
to avoid severe extravasation injury; if extravasation occurs,
phentolamine is used locally to counteract necrosis.

title: DOPAMINE
action:
Acts on dopaminergic receptors (D_1 and D_2) as well as beta-1 and alpha-1 adrenergic
receptors in a dose-dependent manner (renal/mesenteric vasodilation at low doses, cardiac stimulation at
medium doses, and systemic vasoconstriction at high doses).
forms:
Intravenous infusion: 40
mg/mL, 80 mg/mL, 160
mg/mL. Premixed bags:
0.8 mg/mL to 3.2 mg/mL.
indication:
Correction of hemodynamic
imbalances in shock
syndromes due to
myocardial infarction,
trauma, septic
endotoxemia, and
congestive heart failure.
contraindication:
Pheochromocytoma,
uncorrected
tachyarrhythmias, and
ventricular fibrillation.
adverse:
Ectopic beats, tachycardia,
anginal pain,
palpitations, and
gangrene of extremities
at prolonged high doses.
effects:
Nausea, vomiting,
headache, anxiety,
and goosebumps.
notes:
Must be diluted prior to IV administration; monitor blood pressure
and urine output closely.

title: DOBUTAMINE
action:
Direct-acting synthetic inotrope that is a selective beta-1 adrenergic receptor
agonist, with minor beta-2 and alpha-1 activity, producing strong myocardial contractility and
mild vasodilation.
forms:
Solution for IV infusion: 12.5
mg/mL (in 20 mL vials).
Premixed IV bags: 1 mg/mL, 2
mg/mL, 4 mg/mL.
indication:
Short-term management
of adults with cardiac
decompensation due to
depressed contractility
(such as heart failure or
post-cardiac surgery).
contraindication:
Idiopathic hypertrophic
subaortic stenosis
(IHSS) and known
hypersensitivity to
dobutamine.
adverse:
Marked increases in heart rate
or blood pressure,
precipitation of ventricular
arrhythmias, and myocardial
ischemia.
effects:
Increased heart rate,
elevated blood pressure,
headache, nausea, and
shortness of breath.
notes:
Contains sodium bisulﬁte which can cause allergic-type reactions
in susceptible patients; used primarily in short-term hospital
infusions.

title: ISOPROTERENOL
action:
Non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist. It produces profound
chronotropic and inotropic cardiac stimulation alongside systemic vasodilation and bronchodilation.
forms:
Injection solution:
0.2 mg/mL
(1:5000).
indication:
Management of AV nodal
block, Stokes-Adams
attacks, cardiac arrest
(prior to electrical
pacing), and
bronchospasm during
anesthesia.
contraindication:
Tachycardia or heart
block caused by
digitalis toxicity, and
ventricular
arrhythmias
requiring inotropic
therapy.
adverse:
Serious
tachyarrhythmias,
angina pectoris, severe
hypotension, and
cardiac arrest.
effects:
Flushing, sweating,
tachycardia,
palpitations,
nervousness, and
dizziness.
notes:
Largely replaced in modern practice by more selective cardiac
and respiratory agents, but retains utility in speciﬁc
bradyarrhythmia emergencies.

title: PHENYLEPHRINE
action:
Powerful direct-acting alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist that causes marked
arterial vasoconstriction, raising systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and induces mydriasis.
forms:
Injection: 10 mg/mL.
Ophthalmic solution: 2.5%, 10%.
Nasal spray: 0.125%, 0.25%,
0.5%, 1%.
indication:
Treatment of hypotension
during anesthesia, systemic
shock states, paroxysmal
supraventricular
tachycardia, relief of nasal
congestion, and production
of mydriasis for eye exams.
contraindication:
Severe hypertension,
ventricular
tachycardia, narrow-
angle glaucoma, and
concurrent use with
MAO inhibitors.
adverse:
Hypertensive crisis, acute
pulmonary edema, severe
reflex bradycardia, and
cardiac arrhythmias.
effects:
Headache, excitability,
restlessness, reflex
bradycardia, and stinging
upon nasal/eye
application.
notes:
Often triggers reﬂex bradycardia due to the body's baroreceptor
response to sudden, sharp increases in blood pressure.

title: ALBUTEROL
action:
Selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth
muscle by stimulating intracellular adenylate cyclase and increasing cyclic AMP.
forms:
Metered-dose inhaler (MDI): 90 mcg/
actuation.
Nebulization solution: 0.083%, 0.5%.
Oral tablets: 2 mg, 4 mg. Syrup: 2 mg/5
mL.
indication:
Treatment and prevention of
bronchospasm in
reversible obstructive
airway disease (asthma,
COPD) and prevention of
exercise-induced
bronchospasm.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
albuterol
components and
severe
tachyarrhythmias.
adverse:
Paradoxical bronchospasm,
hypokalemia, cardiac
arrhythmias, and severe
hypersensitivity
reactions.
effects:
Tremors, nervousness,
tachycardia,
palpitations, headache,
and throat irritation.
notes:
Widely used as a short-acting rescue inhaler for acute
asthma symptoms.

title: METAPROTERENOL
action:
Relatively selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist that relaxes smooth
muscle of the bronchi, uterus, and vascular bed.
forms:
Inhalation aerosol: 0.65 mg/actuation.
Syrup: 10 mg/5 mL.
Tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg.
indication:
Bronchodilator for
bronchial asthma and
reversible
bronchospasm
associated with
bronchitis and
emphysema.
contraindication:
Cardiac arrhythmias
associated with
tachycardia and
known
hypersensitivity to
sympathomimetic
amines.
adverse:
Tachycardia, palpitations,
hypertension, and
paradoxical
bronchospasm.
effects:
Nervousness, tremor,
nausea, vomiting,
and bad taste in the
mouth.
notes:
Possesses slightly less beta-2 selectivity than albuterol, meaning
it can have a higher incidence of cardiac side eﬀects.

title: TERBUTALINE
action:
Relatively selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist that relaxes bronchial
smooth muscle and inhibits uterine contractions.
forms:
Injection solution: 1 mg/mL.
Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg.
indication:
Prevention and relief of
bronchospasm in
bronchial asthma and
chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease.
contraindication:
Known hypersensitivity to
sympathomimetic
amines and use for
tocolysis (off-label use
restricted due to
maternal cardiac risks).
adverse:
Pulmonary edema (in
obstetric contexts),
maternal/fetal tachycardia,
and cardiac arrhythmias.
effects:
Tremor, nervousness,
headache, tachycardia,
and muscle cramps.
notes:
Black box warnings exist regarding oral use for suppressing
preterm labor due to severe cardiac adverse events.

title:
SALMETEROL, FORMETEROL, INDACATEROL,
VILANTEROL,OLODATEROL
action:
Long-acting, selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonists. They provide prolonged
relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle through high lipid solubility or receptor-binding kinetics
lasting 12 to 24 hours.
forms:
• Salmeterol: Inhalation powder (Diskus) 50 mcg.
• Formoterol: Inhalation capsule/solution 12 mcg.
• Indacaterol: Inhalation powder 75 mcg, 150 mcg.
• Vilanterol: Available in combination inhalers
(e.g., with umeclidinium or fluticasone).
• Olodaterol: Respimat soft mist 2.5 mcg/actuation.
indication:
Long-term, maintenance
treatment of asthma
(always combined with
an inhaled
corticosteroid) and
COPD.
contraindication:
Primary treatment of acute
asthma symptoms
without a concurrent
inhaled corticosteroid
(monotherapy in asthma
carries increased
mortality risk).
adverse:
Severe paradoxical
bronchospasm, life-
threatening asthma
exacerbations (if used
without ICS), and
cardiac arrhythmias.
effects:
Tremor, dizziness,
headache,
tachycardia, and
nasopharyngitis
notes:
These are maintenance agents, not rescue medications; salmeterol
and formoterol should never be used alone to treat acute, sudden
asthma attacks.

title: AMPETHAMINES
action:
Indirect-acting sympathomimetic agents that promote the release of stored catecholamines
(norepinephrine and dopamine) from nerve terminals into the synaptic cleft, while inhibiting their reuptake.
forms:
Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg.
Extended-release capsules: 5 mg to 30 mg.
indication:
Treatment of Attention
Deficit Hyperactivity
Disorder (ADHD) and
narcolepsy.
contraindication:
Advanced arteriosclerosis,
symptomatic cardiovascular
disease, moderate-to-severe
hypertension, hyperthyroidism,
glaucoma, and history of drug
abuse.
adverse:
Psychotic episodes,
cardiomyopathy,
hypertensive crisis, and
severe psychological
dependence/abuse
potential.
effects:
Insomnia, decreased
appetite, weight loss,
dry mouth,
tachycardia, and
nervousness.
notes:
Classiﬁed as Schedule II controlled substances due to high
potential for abuse and psychological dependence.

title: METHAMPETHAMINES
action:
Central nervous system stimulant and indirect sympathomimetic that causes
marked release of dopamine and other monoamines into synapses, blocking their reuptake.
forms: Oral tablets: 5 mg.
indication:
Short-term adjunct in
the management of
exogenous obesity and
treatment of ADHD
(rarely prescribed).
contraindication:
Advanced arteriosclerosis,
symptomatic
cardiovascular disease,
hypertension,
hyperthyroidism, and
history of substance abuse.
adverse:
Severe cardiovascular
toxicity, stroke, paranoia,
hallucinations, and
severe addiction/
dependence.
effects:
Insomnia, irritability,
hyperactive motor
activity, tremor,
sweating, and
anorexia.
notes:
High abuse liability; listed as a Schedule II controlled substance
with tightly restricted clinical indications.

title: EPHEDRINE
action:
Mixed-acting sympathomimetic agent. It directly stimulates alpha and beta
receptors, and indirectly causes the release of endogenous norepinephrine from storage vesicles.
forms:
Injection solution: 50 mg/mL.
Oral capsules: 25 mg, 50 mg.
indication:
Treatment of acute
hypotension,
particularly during
spinal or general
anesthesia, and relief
of bronchospasm.
contraindication:
Angle-closure glaucoma,
concurrent use with
MAO inhibitors,
severe hypertension,
and tachyarrhythmias.
adverse:
Hypertensive crisis,
stroke,
tachyarrhythmias, and
urinary retention.
effects:
Nervousness, insomnia,
dizziness,
palpitations, and
sweating.
notes:
Prone to tachyphylaxis (rapidly diminishing physiological response
with repeated doses due to depletion of stored norepinephrine).

title: COCAINE
action:
Blocks the presynaptic reuptake pump for catecholamines (norepinephrine,
dopamine, and serotonin), resulting in high concentrations of neurotransmitters in synapses. It
also acts as a local anesthetic by blocking sodium channels.
forms:
Topical solution: 4%, 10%
(restricted clinical use).
indication:
Local anesthesia of
mucous membranes of
the oral, laryngeal, and
nasal cavities
(historical/specialized
clinical use).
contraindication:
Known hypersensitivity
to ester-type local
anesthetics, intravenous
or subcutaneous
administration (high
systemic toxicity), and
severe cardiovascular
disease.
adverse:
Severe coronary
vasospasm, myocardial
infarction, stroke,
malignant hyperthermia,
seizures, and ventricular
fibrillation.
effects:
Euphoria, mydriasis,
hypertension,
tachycardia, anxiety,
and local tissue
ischemia.
notes:
Highly addictive controlled substance (Schedule II); clinical use is
restricted strictly to topical mucosal anesthesia where its intrinsic
vasoconstrictive property is advantageous.

title: TYRAMINE
action:
Indirect-acting sympathomimetic amine that enters nerve terminals and displaces stored norepinephrine,
forcing its massive release into the synapse.
forms:
Not an approved
therapeutic drug
product (found naturally
in aged, fermented, or
cured foods like cheese,
wine, and cured meats).
indication:
None clinically (studied
primarily for its adverse
dietary interactions)
contraindication:
Patients taking Monoamine
Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs).
adverse:
Severe, life-threatening
hypertensive crisis ("cheese
effect"), intracranial
hemorrhage, and cardiac
arrhythmias.
effects:
Severe pulsatile
headache,
palpitations,
sweating, nausea,
and vomiting.
notes:
Normally degraded rapidly by MAO enzymes in the gut wall and
liver; patients taking MAOIs cannot break it down, allowing
dietary tyramine to trigger a catastrophic spike in blood pressure.

title: PHENTOLAMINE
action:
Competitive, non-selective alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It
produces vasodilation by blocking alpha-receptors on vascular smooth muscle, lowering peripheral
resistance.
forms:
Intravenous/Intramuscular injection:
5 mg/vial (reconstituted).
Ophthalmic solution: 0.75% (for
mydriasis reversal).
indication:
Prevention or control of
hypertensive episodes due to
pheochromocytoma (such as
during preoperative preparation
or surgical excision), prevention
of dermal necrosis following
norepinephrine extravasation,
and reversal of soft-tissue local
anesthesia.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
phentolamine, coronary
artery disease,
myocardial infarction,
angina pectoris, or a
history of myocardial
infarction.
adverse:
Severe reflex tachycardia,
cardiac arrhythmias,
exacerbation of myocardial
ischemia, angina, and
cerebrovascular spasm.
effects:
Flushing, dizziness, nasal
stuffiness, orthostatic
hypotension, nausea,
and vomiting.
notes:
Frequently inﬁltrated subcutaneously around an area of
norepinephrine extravasation within 12 hours to block localized
vasoconstriction and prevent tissue necrosis.

title: PHENOXYBENZAMINE
action:
Non-competitive, irreversible alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It forms
a stable covalent bond with alpha-receptors, leading to a long-lasting blockade that cannot be overcome by
high concentrations of circulating agonists.
forms: Oral capsules: 10 mg.
indication:
Management of
pheochromocytoma (to control
blood pressure episodes and
symptoms of catecholamine
excess prior to and during
surgery), and chronic urinary
retention due to prostatic
obstruction (off-label).
contraindication:
Conditions where a fall in
blood pressure would be
dangerous (such as
uncompensated heart
failure or severe coronary
artery disease), and
hypersensitivity.
adverse:
Marked postural (orthostatic)
hypotension accompanied
by dizziness or fainting,
reflex tachycardia, and
inhibition of ejaculation.
effects:
Nasal congestion,
miosis, dry mouth,
tiredness, and lethargy.
notes:
Because it binds irreversibly, its blockade lasts for several days
after discontinuation, requiring slow dosage titration and adequate
volume repletion prior to surgical procedures.

title: PRASOZIN
action:
Competitive, selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It blocks postsynaptic
alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle and bladder neck tissue, leading to vasodilation of both
arterioles and veins.
forms:
Oral capsules:
1 mg, 2 mg, 5 mg.
indication:
Management of essential
hypertension, and
treatment of symptoms
related to benign
prostatic hyperplasia
(BPH) and Raynaud's
phenomenon.
contraindication:
Known
hypersensitivity
to quinazolines
or prazosin.
adverse:
Severe "first-dose syncope"
(profound orthostatic
hypotension with sudden loss of
consciousness shortly after the
initial dose), marked dizziness,
and palpitations.
effects:
Dizziness, headache,
drowsiness, weakness,
nausea, and nasal
congestion.
notes:
To minimize the risk of ﬁrst-dose syncope, the initial dose should
be very small (e.g., 1 mg) and taken right before bedtime.

title: DAXAZOSIN, TERASOZIN
action:
Competitive blockade of postsynaptic alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, relaxing smooth muscle in the bladder
neck and prostate capsule (improving urine flow) while dilating peripheral blood vessels (lowering blood pressure).
forms:
• Doxazosin: Tablets: 1 mg, 2 mg, 4 mg, 8
mg;
Extended-release tablets: 4 mg, 8 mg.
• Terazosin: Capsules: 1 mg, 2 mg, 5 mg,
10 mg.
indication:
Treatment of hypertension and
functional symptoms of
benign prostatic hyperplasia
(BPH).
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
quinazolines, doxazosin,
or terazosin, and history
of orthostatic
hypotension.
adverse:
First-dose orthostatic
hypotension, syncope,
priapism (prolonged, painful
erection), and intraoperative
floppy iris syndrome (IFIS)
during cataract surgery.
effects:
Dizziness, fatigue,
peripheral edema,
headache, nasal
congestion, and
asthenia.
notes:
Like prazosin, the ﬁrst dose should be administered at bedtime to
mitigate severe dizziness or sudden fainting spells.

title: TAMSULOSIN, SILODOSIN
action:
Highly selective antagonists for alpha-1A and alpha-1D receptor subtypes located
predominantly in the prostate, prostatic urethra, and bladder base, causing minimal systemic vasodilation
compared to non-subtype selective alpha blockers.
forms:
• Tamsulosin: Capsules (modified
release): 0.4 mg.
• Silodosin: Capsules: 4 mg, 8
mg.
indication:
Treatment of signs and
symptoms of benign
prostatic hyperplasia
(BPH).
contraindication:
Severe hepatic impairment
(for silodosin), severe renal
impairment, and concurrent
use of strong CYP3A4
inhibitors (like
ketoconazole).
adverse:
Severe abnormal ejaculation
(retrograde ejaculation),
orthostatic hypotension (though
less frequent than with
doxazosin/prazosin), and
intraoperative floppy iris
syndrome (IFIS).
effects:
Dizziness, headache,
nasopharyngitis,
rhinitis, and diarrhea.
notes:
Because of their high selectivity for prostate tissue, they have
minimal impact on blood pressure, making dose adjustments for
hypertension unnecessary.

title: YOHIMBINE
action:
Competitive, selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist. By blocking presynaptic
alpha-2 receptors, it increases the release of norepinephrine in the central and peripheral nervous
systems, raising blood pressure, heart rate, and sympathetic tone.
forms:
Oral tablets: 5.4 mg
(formulations vary widely as
prescription medications or
herbal/dietary supplements).
indication:
Historically used for
the management of
erectile dysfunction
and orthostatic
hypotension.
contraindication:
Renal disease,
cardiorenal
dysfunction, history
of ulcer disease,
psychiatric disorders,
and hypertension.
adverse:
Hypertensive crisis,
severe anxiety, panic
attacks, tachycardia,
and motor tremors.
effects:
Headaches, dizziness,
nervousness, irritability,
nausea, and frequent
urination.
notes:
It is a naturally occurring alkaloid (from the bark of Pausinystalia
yohimbe) that can trigger severe central nervous system excitation
and pronounced blood pressure spikes.

title: PROPANOLOL
action:
Non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist with membrane-
stabilizing activity. It blocks the chronotropic, inotropic, and vasodilatory responses to beta-adrenergic
stimulation and crosses the blood-brain barrier easily.
forms:
Oral tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg, 40
mg, 60 mg, 80 mg.
Extended-release capsules: 60 mg,
80 mg, 120 mg, 160 mg.
Injection: 1 mg/mL.
indication:
Hypertension, angina pectoris,
cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial
infarction prophylaxis, migraine
headache prophylaxis, essential
tremor, and management of
hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis
symptoms.
contraindication:
Bronchial asthma, severe
chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease (COPD),
sinus bradycardia, second-
or third-degree heart block,
cardiogenic shock, and
overt heart failure.
adverse:
Severe bronchospasm, heart block,
severe bradycardia, precipitation
of congestive heart failure, and
severe rebound hypertension if
abruptly withdrawn
effects:
Fatigue, cold extremities,
sleep disturbances,
vivid dreams,
depression, and sexual
dysfunction.
notes:
Never stop therapy abruptly; beta-blockers must be tapered over 1
to 2 weeks to avoid rebound tachycardia or myocardial ischemia.

title: TIMOLOL, BETAXOLOL
action:
Competitive beta-adrenergic receptor blockers that reduce the production of aqueous humor
in the ciliary epithelium of the eye, lowering intraocular pressure. Systemically, they block beta receptors to
lower heart rate and contractility
forms:
• Timolol: Ophthalmic solution:
0.25%, 0.5%.
Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg.
• Betaxolol: Ophthalmic solution:
0.5%.
Oral tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg
indication:
Treatment of chronic
open-angle glaucoma
and ocular hypertension;
systemic forms are used
for hypertension and
migraine prevention.
contraindication:
Asthma, history of severe
chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease, sinus
bradycardia, and
cardiogenic shock.
adverse:
Systemic absorption from
eye drops causing severe
bronchospasm,
bradycardia, heart block,
and heart failure flare-
ups.
effects:
Stinging or burning
upon eye drop
instillation, blurred
vision, dry eyes,
fatigue, and headache.
notes:
applying eye drops, patients should use nasolacrimal occlusion
(gentle tearing duct compression) to minimize systemic absorption
into the bloodstream.

title: PINDOLOL
action:
Non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist with significant Intrinsic Sympathomimetic
Activity (ISA) (partial agonist activity), meaning it blocks strong catecholamines while providing mild
baseline stimulation of beta receptors itself
forms:
Oral tablets:
5 mg, 10 mg.
indication:
Management of
essential
hypertension.
contraindication:
Bronchial asthma,
cardiogenic shock,
second- and third-
degree heart block,
and severe
bradycardia.
adverse:
Severe bronchospasm,
heart block, and acute
worsening of heart failure
in susceptible patients.
effects:
Dizziness, weakness, insomnia,
vivid dreams, muscle pain, and
lower incidence of resting
bradycardia compared to other
beta blockers.
notes:
Due to its intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA), it causes less
resting bradycardia and cold-extremity side eﬀects than pure
antagonists like propranolol

title: NADOLOL
action:
Long-acting, non-selective beta-adrenergic receptor blocker without
membrane-stabilizing activity or significant intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.
forms:
Oral tablets: 20
mg, 40 mg, 80
mg, 120 mg,
160 mg.
indication:
Management of
hypertension and
long-term
prophylactic
treatment of angina
pectoris.
contraindication:
Bronchial asthma,
cardiogenic shock,
sinus bradycardia,
and greater than first-
degree heart block.
adverse:
Severe bradycardia,
heart block,
precipitating heart
failure, and acute
bronchoconstriction.
effects:
Fatigue, dizziness,
bradycardia, cold
extremities, and
emotional depression.
notes:
Excreted primarily unchanged by the kidneys, meaning dosing
intervals must be extended signiﬁcantly in patients with renal
impairment.

title: ATENOLOL
action:
Cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist that preferentially blocks beta-1
receptors in the heart, reducing heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure, with less effect on bronchial and
vascular beta-2 receptors at lower doses.
forms:
Oral tablets: 25 mg, 50
mg, 100 mg.
Intravenous injection:
0.5 mg/mL.
indication:
Management of
hypertension, long-
term management of
angina pectoris, and
secondary prevention
of myocardial
infarction.
contraindication:
Sinus bradycardia,
heart block greater
than first degree,
cardiogenic shock,
and overt cardiac
failure.
adverse:
Symptomatic bradycardia,
severe heart block, heart
failure exacerbation, and
bronchospasm (at high
doses due to loss of
selectivity).
effects:
Cold hands and feet,
fatigue, dizziness,
lethargy, and diarrhea
notes:
Hydrophilic agent eliminated primarily by the kidneys; requires
dosage reduction in patients with renal function impairment.

title: ESMOLOL
action:
Ultra-short-acting, cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It
inhibits beta-1 receptors in the heart, reducing heart rate and myocardial contractility.
forms:
Intravenous injection / infusion: 10
mg/mL, 250 mg/mL.
Premixed infusion bags: 10 mg/mL,
20 mg/mL.
indication:
Rapid, short-term control of
ventricular rate in patients
with atrial fibrillation or
atrial flutter, and treatment
of perioperative
hypertension and
tachycardia.
contraindication:
Sinus bradycardia,
severe cardiogenic
shock, uncompensated
heart failure, and pre-
existing pulmonary
hypertension.
adverse:
Severe hypotension,
profound bradycardia,
cardiac arrest, and local
infusion-site
inflammation or necrosis.
effects:
Asymptomatic or
symptomatic hypotension,
diaphoresis, dizziness,
and nausea.
notes:
Features an extremely short elimination half-life of approximately
9 minutes, allowing rapid titration and quick reversal of eﬀects if
adverse reactions occur.

title: METOPROLOL
action:
Selective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist that reduces heart rate,
cardiac output, and blood pressure.
forms:
• Metoprolol tartrate: Tablets: 25 mg, 50
mg, 100 mg.
Injection: 1 mg/mL.
• Metoprolol succinate (ER):
Extended-release tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg,
100 mg, 200 mg.
indication:
Hypertension, angina
pectoris, heart failure
(succinate form), and
early intervention in
acute myocardial
infarction
contraindication:
Severe bradycardia,
heart block greater
than first degree,
cardiogenic shock, and
decompensated heart
failure.
adverse:
Severe bradycardia,
hypotension, heart block,
and exacerbation of
asthma or heart failure.
effects:
Fatigue, dizziness,
depression, diarrhea,
shortness of breath,
and bradycardia.
notes:
Metoprolol tartrate is typically taken twice daily with meals, while
the succinate formulation is designed for convenient once-daily
dosing.

title: NEBIVOLOL
action:
Highly cardioselective beta-1 receptor blocker that also promotes endothelial nitric
oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation, reducing peripheral vascular resistance without typical beta-
blocker-induced cold extremities.
forms:
Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 5
mg, 10 mg, 20 mg.
indication:
Treatment of essential
hypertension, alone or
in combination with
other agents, to lower
blood pressure and
reduce cardiovascular
risk.
contraindication:
Severe bradycardia,
heart block greater
than first degree,
cardiogenic shock,
decompensated heart
failure, and severe
hepatic impairment.
adverse:
Severe hypotension,
acute heart failure
worsening, and AV
block.
effects:
Headache, fatigue,
dizziness, diarrhea,
nausea, and
insomnia.
notes:
Its unique nitric oxide-releasing property sets it apart from
traditional beta-1 blockers by avoiding adverse metabolic proﬁles
and peripheral vasoconstriction.

title: BUTOXAMINE
action:
Selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It blocks beta-2 receptors, causing
inhibition of beta-2-mediated vasodilation, bronchodilation, and glycogenolysis.
forms:
Research chemical / specialized
pharmacological tool (not an
approved commercial therapeutic
pharmaceutical drug).
indication:
None clinically approved
(used primarily as an
experimental
pharmacological tool to
study beta-2 adrenergic
pathways).
contraindication:
N/A (Not used in
human clinical
therapeutics).
adverse:
Pronounced
bronchoconstriction and
metabolic disturbances if
administered systemically.
effects:
Increased airway
resistance and
muscle cramping.
notes:
Primarily of academic and pharmacological value to isolate
beta-2 responses in laboratory settings; not utilized in clinical
patient care.

title: LABETALOL
action:
Competitive antagonist at alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors. It produces
peripheral vasodilation (via alpha-1 block) while preventing reflex tachycardia through simultaneous
beta-blockade.
forms:
Oral tablets: 100 mg, 200 mg,
300 mg.
Intravenous injection: 5 mg/mL.
indication:
Management of essential
hypertension,
hypertensive
emergencies, and blood
pressure control during
pregnancy-induced
hypertension
(preeclampsia).
contraindication:
Bronchial asthma, overt
cardiac failure, greater
than first-degree heart
block, cardiogenic
shock, and severe
bradycardia.
adverse:
Severe orthostatic
hypotension, acute
bronchospasm, heart block,
and hepatocellular injury
(liver damage).
effects:
Dizziness, fatigue,
nausea, scalp tingling,
nasal stuffiness, and
vivid dreams.
notes:
Widely utilized in obstetrics for hypertensive crises during
pregnancy because it reduces blood pressure eﬀectively without
heavily compromising uteroplacental blood ﬂow.

title: CAVEDILOL
action:
Non-selective beta blocker and alpha-1 blocker with antioxidant properties. It
blocks beta-1, beta-2, and alpha-1 receptors, causing vasodilation and reducing cardiac workload.
forms:
Oral tablets: 3.125 mg, 6.25 mg, 12.5
mg, 25 mg.
Extended-release capsules: 10 mg, 20
mg, 40 mg, 80 mg.
indication:
Management of mild to
severe chronic heart
failure, left ventricular
dysfunction following
myocardial infarction, and
essential hypertension.
contraindication:
Decompensated heart
failure requiring
intravenous inotropes,
bronchial asthma, second-
or third-degree AV block,
and severe hepatic
impairment.
adverse:
Severe hypotension,
worsening heart failure
symptoms during
initiation, bradycardia,
and bronchospasm
effects:
Dizziness, fatigue,
weight gain, diarrhea,
hyperlipidemia, and
hyperglycemia.
notes:
Must be taken with food to slow absorption rate and minimize
the risk of sudden orthostatic hypotension or dizziness

title: HYDROCHLOROTHIAZIDE
action:
Thiazide diuretic that inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal
convoluted tubule of the nephron, increasing the excretion of sodium, water, chloride, and
potassium.
forms:
Oral tablets: 12.5 mg, 25 mg,
50 mg.
Oral solution: 50 mg/5 mL.
indication:
Management of essential
hypertension and edema
associated with
congestive heart failure,
hepatic cirrhosis, and
corticosteroid/estrogen
therapy.
contraindication:
Anuria,
hypersensitivity to
sulfonamide-derived
drugs, and severe
renal or hepatic
impairment.
adverse:
Severe hypokalemia,
hyponatremia, hyperglycemia,
hyperuricemia, acute angle-
closure glaucoma, and severe
hypersensitivity skin reactions
(Stevens-Johnson syndrome).
effects:
Frequent urination,
dizziness, lightheadedness,
mild orthostatic
hypotension, headache,
and fatigue.
notes:
Sulfa-allergic patients may cross-react with thiazides; can elevate
blood glucose and uric acid levels.

title: CHLORTHALIDONE
action:
Thiazide-like diuretic that inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the
cortical diluting segment of the ascending loop of Henle and distal tubule, reducing extracellular
fluid volume.
forms:
Oral tablets: 12.5 mg,
25 mg, 50 mg, 100
mg.
indication:
Treatment of
hypertension (as step-
one therapy or add-on)
and management of
edema associated with
heart failure or renal
dysfunction.
contraindication:
Anuria, hypersensitivity
to sulfonamides or
chlorthalidone, and
severe electrolyte
depletions.
adverse:
Hypokalemia, severe
hypochloremic alkalosis,
hypercalcemia,
agranulocytosis, aplastic
anemia, and exacerbation of
gout.
effects:
Dizziness, vertigo,
paresthesias, headache,
anorexia, nausea, vomiting,
and increased urination
frequency
notes:
Possesses a signiﬁcantly longer duration of action (up to 72 hours)
compared to standard hydrochlorothiazide

title: FUROSEMIDE
action:
Loop diuretic that inhibits the co-transport system (Na^+/K^+/2Cl^-) in the
thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, promoting massive excretion of water, sodium,
chloride, calcium, and magnesium.
forms:
Oral tablets: 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg.
Oral solution: 8 mg/mL, 10 mg/mL.
Injection solution: 10 mg/mL.
indication:
Treatment of acute
pulmonary edema,
edema associated with
heart failure, hepatic
cirrhosis, renal disease,
and severe hypertension.
contraindication:
Anuria, hepatic coma,
severe electrolyte
depletion, and known
hypersensitivity to
furosemide or
sulfonamides.
adverse:
Profound volume depletion,
circulatory collapse, severe
hypokalemia, ototoxicity
(tinnitus/hearing loss), and
thrombotic events.
effects:
Increased urination
frequency, dizziness,
lightheadedness,
nausea, dyspepsia, and
blurred vision.
notes:
Rapid IV administration can trigger transient or permanent
ototoxicity; patients should be monitored closely for signs of severe
dehydration.

title: SPIRONALACTONE
action:
Potassium-sparing diuretic and competitive mineralocorticoid receptor
antagonist that blocks aldosterone binding in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts,
increasing sodium and water excretion while retaining potassium.
forms:
Oral tablets: 25 mg,
50 mg, 100 mg.
indication:
Management of heart
failure with reduced
ejection fraction,
resistant hypertension,
primary
hyperaldosteronism, and
edema due to cirrhosis
or nephrotic syndrome.
contraindication:
Acute renal
insufficiency,
anuria,
hyperkalemia, and
concurrent use of
eplerenone.
adverse:
Severe hyperkalemia,
metabolic acidosis,
agranulocytosis, and
acute renal dysfunction.
effects:
Gynecomastia, breast
pain/tenderness,
menstrual irregularities,
dizziness, lethargy, and
mild gastrointestinal
cramps.
notes:
Unique for being a potassium-sparing diuretic that can cause
endocrine side eﬀects (such as gynecomastia in men) due to its
secondary anti-androgen activity.

title: CLONIDINE
action:
Central alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist. It stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the
brainstem vasomotor center, reducing sympathetic outflow from the central nervous system,
which lowers peripheral resistance, heart rate, and blood pressure.
forms:
Oral tablets: 0.1 mg, 0.2 mg, 0.3 mg.
Transdermal patches (weekly): 0.1
mg/24hr, 0.2 mg/24hr, 0.3 mg/
24hr.
Injection solution: 100 mcg/mL.
indication:
Management of essential
hypertension, attention deficit
hyperactivity disorder
(ADHD - off-label/specific
formulations), and
management of severe cancer
pain or opioid withdrawal
symptoms.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity to
clonidine and severe
sinus bradycardia or
AV block (unless a
functioning
pacemaker is
present).
adverse:
Severe rebound hypertension
upon abrupt
discontinuation, profound
bradycardia, and depressive
symptoms.
effects:
Dry mouth, drowsiness,
sedation, dizziness,
constipation, fatigue,
and sexual dysfunction.
notes:
Must never be stopped abruptly; sudden withdrawal can trigger a
dangerous hypertensive crisis characterized by extreme surges in
catecholamines.

title: METHYLDOPA
action:
Central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. It is metabolized intracellularly to
alphamethylnorepinephrine, which replaces norepinephrine in vesicles and stimulates central inhibitory alpha-2
receptors, reducing sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow.
forms:
Oral tablets: 250 mg, 500 mg.
Intravenous injection: 50 mg/
mL.
indication:
Management of
hypertension, including
hypertension during
pregnancy
(preeclampsia/
gestational
hypertension).
contraindication:
Active hepatic disease
(such as acute hepatitis
or active cirrhosis),
previous methyldopa-
induced liver disorders,
and concurrent use with
monoamine oxidase
inhibitors (MAOIs).
adverse:
Drug-induced immune
hemolytic anemia
(positive direct Coombs
test), severe hepatitis, liver
necrosis, and parkinsonian
signs.
effects:
Drowsiness, sedation, dry
mouth, nasal stuffiness,
edema, dizziness, and
postpartum depression.
notes:
Widely preferred historically and currently for treating hypertension
during pregnancy due to its well-established fetal safety proﬁle,
despite routine monitoring required for liver enzymes and Coombs-
positive hemolytic anemia.

title: HEXAMETHONIUM
action:
Non-depolarizing ganglionic blocker that competitively blocks nicotinic
acetylcholine receptors located in both sympathetic and parasympathetic autonomic ganglia.
forms:
Historical drug; rarely or
no longer manufactured
for commercial clinical
distribution
indication:
Historically used as
an antihypertensive
agent (obsolete due
to severe adverse
autonomic blocking
effects).
contraindication:
Severe
hypotension,
coronary
insufficiency, and
paralytic ileus.
adverse:
Profound orthostatic
hypotension,
cardiovascular collapse,
paralytic ileus, and severe
urinary retention.
effects:
Cycloplegia, dry
mouth, severe
constipation,
impotence, and
dizziness.
notes:
It blocks both sympathetic and parasympathetic outﬂows entirely,
resulting in unpredictable and severe side eﬀects. It is primarily of
historical and pharmacological interest today.

title: TRIMETHAPHAN
action:
Short-acting competitive ganglionic blocking agent that blocks transmission
through autonomic ganglia, causing vasodilation and a marked drop in blood pressure.
forms:
Intravenous infusion
solution: 50 mg/mL.
indication:
Production of controlled
hypotension during specific
surgical procedures (such as
neurosurgery or repair of
coarctation of the aorta) and
management of hypertensive
emergencies.
contraindication:
Hypovolemia, shock,
severe anemia,
asphyxia, and
respiratory
insufficiency.
adverse:
Severe, unmanageable
hypotension,
respiratory
depression, and
paralytic ileus.
effects:
Mydriasis, cycloplegia,
urinary retention, dry
mouth, and cessation
of bowel sounds.
notes:
Administered strictly via continuous IV infusion under close
blood pressure monitoring; eﬀects wear oﬀ rapidly upon
discontinuation.

title: MECAMYLAMINE
action:
Non-selective, non-competitive ganglionic blocker that crosses the
blood-brain barrier readily to block nicotinic receptors in autonomic ganglia and the central
nervous system.
forms:
Oral tablets: 2.5 mg
(historically; current
clinical availability is
specialized/limited).
indication:
Historically used for
moderately severe to
severe essential
hypertension;
investigated as an
adjunct for tobacco
smoking cessation and
Tourette's syndrome
contraindication:
Coronary
thrombosis, recent
myocardial
infarction, uremia,
and organic
cerebral damage.
adverse:
Severe orthostatic
hypotension,
neuromuscular weakness,
and toxic psychosis /
convulsions (due to CNS
penetration).
effects:
Constipation (can
progress to paralytic
ileus), blurred vision,
dry mouth, urinary
retention, and sedation.
notes:
Unlike many other ganglion blockers, it is absorbed well orally
due to its secondary amine structure, which also allows it to
enter the central nervous system easily.

title: RESERPINE
action:
Inhibits the transport of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin into
storage vesicles (VMAT2) within postganglionic sympathetic nerve endings, leading to
depletion of peripheral and central monoamine stores.
forms:
Oral tablets: 0.1
mg, 0.25 mg.
indication:
Management of
essential
hypertension
(historically
common, now
specialized).
contraindication:
Known
hypersensitivity,
history of mental
depression
(especially with
suicidal tendencies),
active peptic ulcer
disease, ulcerative
colitis, and
concurrent use with
MAO inhibitors.
adverse:
Severe depressive
states, psychic
depression, Parkinson-
like extrapyramidal
symptoms, peptic ulcer
activation, and severe
bradycardia.
effects:
Nasal congestion,
drowsiness, dizziness,
lethargy, diarrhea,
impotence, and weight
gain
notes:
Can cross the blood-brain barrier easily, which accounts for its
signiﬁcant central nervous system side eﬀects, including severe
mental depression.

title: GUANADREL
action:
Adrenergic neuron blocker that accumulates in sympathetic nerve
terminals and replaces norepinephrine in storage vesicles, blocking the release of
norepinephrine in response to nerve stimulation.
forms:
Oral tablets: 10
mg, 25 mg.
indication:
Management of
moderate to severe
essential
hypertension
(typically for
patients
unresponsive to
other agents).
contraindication:
Established or
suspected
pheochromocytoma,
congestive heart
failure, concurrent use
with MAO inhibitors,
and severe coronary
artery disease.
adverse:
Marked orthostatic
hypotension, severe
syncope, and
exacerbation of heart
failure.
effects:
Exertional dizziness,
daytime fatigue, diarrhea,
ﬂuid retention, peripheral
edema, and sexual
dysfunction.
notes:
Prone to causing pronounced orthostatic hypotension, especially
upon standing up or exercising.

title: PRAZOSIN
action:
Competitive, selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor
antagonist that relaxes vascular smooth muscle and bladder neck tissue.
forms:
Oral capsules: 1
mg, 2 mg, 5 mg.
indication:
Essential
hypertension,
benign prostatic
hyperplasia (BPH)
symptoms, and
Raynaud's
phenomenon.
contraindication:
Hypersensitivity
to quinazolines
or prazosin.
adverse:
First-dose syncope
(severe orthostatic
hypotension with
sudden loss of
consciousness), marked
dizziness, and
palpitations.
effects:
Dizziness,
headache,
drowsiness,
weakness, and
nasal congestion.
notes:
The ﬁrst dose should always be taken at bedtime to prevent
sudden fainting episodes.

title: DOXASOXIN
action:
Selective alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist that produces vasodilation
and relaxes smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate.
forms:
Oral tablets: 1 mg, 2 mg,
4 mg, 8 mg.
Extended-release tablets:
4 mg, 8 mg
indication:
Treatment of
hypertension and
symptoms of
benign prostatic
hyperplasia
(BPH).
contraindication:
History of
orthostatic
hypotension and
hypersensitivity to
quinazolines
adverse:
Severe orthostatic
hypotension,
syncope, priapism,
and intraoperative
ﬂoppy iris syndrome
(IFIS).
effects:
Dizziness, fatigue,
edema, headache,
and vertigo.
notes:
Like prazosin, initial dosing should start low and be taken at
bedtime to mitigate acute postural blood pressure drops.

title: PROPANOLOL
action:
Non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptor
antagonist with membrane-stabilizing activity.
forms:
Oral tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, 80
mg.
Extended-release capsules: 60 mg, 80
mg, 120 mg, 160 mg.
Injection: 1 mg/mL.
indication:
Hypertension, angina
pectoris, cardiac
arrhythmias,
migraine
prophylaxis, essential
tremor, and
hyperthyroidism
symptoms.
contraindication:
Bronchial asthma,
severe COPD,
sinus bradycardia,
second- or third-
degree heart block,
and cardiogenic
shock.
adverse:
Severe bronchospasm,
heart block, profound
bradycardia, and acute
heart failure
exacerbation
effects:
Fatigue, cold
extremities, vivid
dreams, depression,
and sleep
disturbances
notes:
Must never be discontinued abruptly; tapering over 1 to 2 weeks is
mandatory to prevent rebound hypertension or myocardial
ischemia.

title: ATENOLOL
action:
Cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist
that reduces heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure.
forms:
Oral tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg, 100
mg.
Intravenous injection: 0.5 mg/mL.
indication:
Management of
essential
hypertension,
angina pectoris, and
acute myocardial
infarction.
contraindication:
Sinus bradycardia,
heart block greater
than ﬁrst degree,
cardiogenic shock,
and overt heart
failure.
adverse:
Symptomatic
bradycardia, severe
heart block, heart
failure ﬂare-up, and
bronchospasm (at
high doses).
effects:
Cold hands and feet,
fatigue, dizziness, and
lethargy.
notes:
Hydrophilic agent eliminated primarily via the kidneys, requiring
dosage adjustments in renal impairment.

title: LABETOLOL
action:
Competitive antagonist at alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic
receptors, providing peripheral vasodilation and beta-blockade.
forms:
Oral tablets: 100 mg, 200 mg, 300 mg.
Intravenous injection: 5 mg/mL.
indication:
Essential
hypertension,
hypertensive
emergencies, and
pregnancy-induced
hypertension
(preeclampsia).
contraindication:
Bronchial asthma,
overt cardiac
failure, greater
than ﬁrst-degree
heart block, and
cardiogenic shock.
adverse:
Severe orthostatic
hypotension,
bronchospasm, heart
block, and
hepatocellular injury
(liver damage).
effects:
Dizziness, fatigue,
nausea, scalp
tingling, and nasal
stuﬃness.
notes:
Frequently used in obstetrics because it lowers blood pressure
safely without signiﬁcantly compromising uteroplacental blood
ﬂow.

title: NIFEDIPINE
action:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits the
transmembrane inﬂux of calcium ions into vascular smooth muscle and cardiac
muscle, leading to coronary and peripheral vasodilation.
forms:
Extended-release/sustained-release
tablets: 30 mg, 60 mg, 90 mg.
Capsules (immediate-release): 10
mg, 20 mg.
indication:
Management of
hypertension,
vasospastic
angina, and
chronic stable
angina.
contraindication:
Known
hypersensitivity to
dihydropyridines,
cardiogenic shock,
and use of
immediate-release
formulations for
acute hypertension
management.
adverse:
Severe hypotension, reflex
tachycardia, myocardial
ischemia (with rapid-acting
forms), and peripheral
edema.
effects:
Flushing,
headache,
dizziness,
peripheral ankle
edema, and fatigue
notes:
Immediate-release capsules are no longer recommended for routine
hypertension control due to risks associated with sudden, sharp blood
pressure drops and reflex tachycardia.

title: VERAPAMIL
action:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits calcium ion
inﬂux into myocardial and vascular smooth muscle cells, slowing AV nodal
conduction and dilating coronary/peripheral vessels
forms:
Oral tablets: 40 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg.
Sustained-release tablets: 120 mg, 180
mg, 240 mg.
Intravenous injection: 2.5 mg/mL.
indication:
Treatment of essential
hypertension, angina
pectoris, and
supraventricular
tachyarrhythmias (such
as atrial ﬁbrillation rate
control).
contraindication:
Severe hypotension,
cardiogenic shock,
second- or third-degree
AV block, sick sinus
syndrome, and
ventricular tachycardia.
adverse:
Severe heart block,
profound bradycardia,
acute heart failure
exacerbation, and
cardiovascular collapse.
effects:
Constipation (very
common), dizziness,
nausea, headache,
and peripheral
edema.
notes:
Prominent negative inotropic and dromotropic eﬀects; should not
be combined with beta-blockers without close clinical monitoring
due to the risk of severe heart block or bradycardia.

title: HYDRALAZINE
action:
Direct-acting arterial vasodilator that relaxes vascular smooth
muscle primarily in arterioles, decreasing systemic vascular resistance
forms:
Oral tablets: 10 mg, 25 mg, 50
mg, 100 mg.
Intravenous/Intramuscular
injection: 20 mg/mL.
indication:
Management of
moderate to severe
essential
hypertension,
hypertensive
emergencies, and
heart failure (often
combined with
isosorbide dinitrate).
contraindication:
Coronary artery
disease, mitral
valvular rheumatic
heart disease, and
